title: Made my first game-ready animated character with AI - free for anyone to use (idle, walk, jump, death)
author: Additional-Put-9294
selftext:
My first asset pack! A hooded assassin character with full animations - idle, walking in 4 directions, jump and death. 128x128 PNG frames with transparent backgrounds, plus sprite strips for easy engine import.



100% free download, free for personal and commercial game projects.



Download: [https://gaurisomesh.itch.io/hooded-assassin](https://gaurisomesh.itch.io/hooded-assassin)



Feedback welcome - planning more characters in the same style. Happy to share my workflow if anyone's curious!

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Seems like there's a bit of nonsense in the side walk cycle. Someone mentioned feet getting cut off, but the worst part is that the leg position is completely random.

First frame - front leg forward, back leg back.  
2nd - Front leg forward (same place), back leg back (same place)  
3rd - Front leg slightly forward, back leg slightly back.  
4th - Front leg all the way forward again, back leg back again!  
5th - Front leg STILL forward and back leg still back.

There was never a swap between legs. The entire thing is just going to look like a random stuttering at best.

Your away walk cycle has the head cut off. Feet once again don't have consistency in placement, though it's not as immediately noticeable. You want an even spread to show smooth omvement but we just kind of have a random height variation. You'd probably be better off just picking two frames here and having one with right foot up, and other with left foot up. The rest is basically wasted noise that's going to make it unreliable (same can be said for the forward walk cycle which has the same issues).

Size variation in your character's fall animation would lead to some serious readability issues. Unless you're intentionally squeezing or stretching (which should be done in engine, not on spritesheet) consistent animations are key. You also have another issue with a clipped head on your jump, and it's odd for him to land on both legs and then suddenly turn that landing into a frame with one leg forward and him resting on his other knee. Physically I'm not sure how that would occur unless his back foot had still been extended in that second to last jump frame.

If you're going to use AI image gens to create your frames, I suggest starting with very basic animations. Try getting two frame animations to look good for repetitive things like a walk cycle, where you switch between the two extremes of the pose, until you get a feel for what you're looking for. For other animations, focus on the anticipation frame and the follow through frame, and consider filling in a frame here or there where you want to smooth out a specific part of it or emphasize a minor action within (like having the anticipation frame be a character reaching down to grasp the katana at their waist. You have that run for .3 seconds, then maybe have one frame with a slight tweak where they tilt the hilt off to the side which lasts for .2 seconds, and then you have a follow through animation which is their sword fully extended in a slash which comes in at that .5 second mark and you have last for .5 seconds (punctuating that frame appearing with an in-engine hit stop alongside some kind of large slash VFX that strikes through the creature and punctuates the weapon trail (that never actually occurred, but our eyes trick us into thinking it did.)

  
You're not then trying to have the AI create 8 frames that all make sense next to one another. AI can't do that. It's horrendous at it. The best you can do is use a video gen and extract the appropriate frames , and then the quality is often quite poor. But if you're using imagegen, you need the different poses to be distinctly different enough in a way that you can keep track of what's going on and prevent stuttering movement. Better to have no movement for a few hundred milliseconds between frames than to have frames that do not properly smooth into one another. Anyone who has seen Into the Spiderverse can attest to how good choppy animation looks when it's properly executed. Another example of this done fairly well is the game Montabi. I don't think any animation the sprites use has more than 3 frames and it feels quite good.

Sorry for all the critique. Good luck.

replies.author: Additional-Put-9294
replies.body: This is honestly one of the most useful comments I've received - thank you for taking the time. You're right about the missing leg swap; I never broke the cycle down frame by frame like that. Hood clipping is already fixed in the 1.1 update that's live now, and I'm reworking the walk cycles next using your two-extremes approach before I add more characters. Saving this comment as my QA checklist.

comments.author: Bananaboy1107
comments.body:
I’m honestly not much of an artist, and I’ve never used Spine, so sprite animation has been one of the most painful parts of making my indie game.

I tried a bunch of AI image tools, but there was always something off — inconsistent characters, weird poses, frames that didn’t flow well, etc.

Eventually I got frustrated enough that I started building my own tool specifically for generating animation frames: [https://www.bananagpt.ai/](https://www.bananagpt.ai/)

It’s definitely not perfect yet, but it’s already made the process a lot easier for me. I’m still improving it as I work on my own game, so feedback from other indie devs would genuinely be helpful.
